newsitem.title: USA: Many U.S. boomers expect to work in old age.
newsitem.headline: Many U.S. boomers expect to work in old age.

text.p: Most U.S. baby boomers expect to be active in their golden years, but more than a third fear they will have to work past the age of 65 to meet their financial needs, according to a study released Tuesday.
As the generation born between 1946 and 1964 approaches their elderly years, most have not reconciled their dreams of travel and leisure with economic realities, one of the authors of the study said.

"They see themselves having a very pro-active retirement that is going to be nothing like their parents'," said Dr. Christopher Hayes, executive director of retirement research at Southhampton College of Long Island University, which conducted the study.
"At the same time, they have not even begun to understand how to fund, or how to economically prepare for those years," he said. "There's a major disconnect."

Nearly half of 1,140 baby boomers surveyed, all with household incomes of at least $30,000, expected to have to work past the traditional retirement age of 65, according to the survey, sponsored by mutual fund firm Scudder, Stevens & Clark, Inc.
A further 13 percent planned to stay with their current careers past age 65, while 20 percent were not planning to retire at all.

A third of the boomers believed that their retirement will be less financially secure than their parents. Surprisingly, those feelings were stronger among college graduates and those who learned to begin savings during childhood.

"It would not surprise me, based upon this study, that as much as 70 percent of baby boomers are going to have to be working in jobs (past age 65) because of economic needs," Hayes said. "They are going to be the first generation that is going to be working well into their 70s."

Two-thirds of baby boomers believe they will meet their long-term financial needs, but they have saved on average only $35,000 for retirement, far less than the $1 million financial planners often state is needed, he said.

Despite average annual income of $56,000 among respondents, three-quarters believed they had little money left to save for retirement after meeting other costs, such as taxes, health care expenses and their childrens' education.
About half confessed to being financially illiterate.
Financial planners must communicate better, emphasizing how much people need to save today for all their financial goals, including retirement in the future.
"What we need to start doing is changing the message. We need to start creating greater incentives to save," Hayes said.
